summary.text: Using multiplicativity of the divisor-sum function, the proof first derives Euler’s form for an even perfect number: \(n=2^kq\), where \(q=2^{k+1}-1\) is prime. The proper divisors include \(1,2,\ldots,2^k\) and \(q,2q,\ldots,2^{k-1}q\), so writing each \(x<n\) as \(x=qy+r\) and using binary expansions of \(y\) and \(r\) realizes every \(x\) as a distinct-divisor sum, while perfection realizes \(n\) itself and bounds all such sums by \(n\); hence the sums are exactly \(0,1,\ldots,n\).

full_proof.text:
Let \(D(n)\) denote the finite set of positive proper divisors of \(n\), and let
\[
\mathcal S(n)=\left\{\sum_{d\in E}d: E\subseteq D(n)\right\}.
\]
Thus \(\mathcal S(n)\) includes the sum of the empty subset, namely \(0\). By definition,
\[
a(n)=|\mathcal S(n)|-1.
\]
We prove that if \(n\) is an even perfect number, then
\[
\mathcal S(n)=\{0,1,\ldots,n\}.
\]
It will then follow immediately that \(|\mathcal S(n)|=n+1\), and hence \(a(n)=n\).

We first derive the form of an even perfect number that will be needed in the subset-sum argument.

Because a perfect number is positive, write
\[
n=2^k m,
\]
where \(m\) is odd and \(k\ge 0\). Since \(n\) is even, in fact \(k\ge 1\). Let \(\sigma(t)\) be the sum of all positive divisors of \(t\). The factors \(2^k\) and \(m\) are coprime, so the divisor-sum function is multiplicative on them:
\[
\sigma(n)=\sigma(2^k)\sigma(m).
\]
Indeed, when two positive integers are coprime, every divisor of their product is uniquely a product of a divisor of the first and a divisor of the second, and summing these products gives the displayed factorization. Also,
\[
\sigma(2^k)=1+2+\cdots+2^k=2^{k+1}-1.
\]
Set
\[
q=2^{k+1}-1.
\]
Since \(n\) is perfect, the sum of its proper divisors is \(n\), and therefore the sum of all its divisors is \(2n\). Consequently,
\[
q\,\sigma(m)=\sigma(n)=2n=2^{k+1}m=(q+1)m.
\]
Let \(s\) be the sum of the proper divisors of \(m\), so that \(\sigma(m)=m+s\). Substitution and cancellation give
\[
q(m+s)=(q+1)m,
\]
whence
\[
qs=m. \tag{1}
\]
Because \(k\ge1\), we have \(q=2^{k+1}-1>1\). Equation (1), together with \(m>0\), shows that \(s>0\). We claim that \(s=1\). If instead \(s>1\), then (1) says that \(s\mid m\), and because \(q>1\), it also says \(s<m\). Thus both \(1\) and \(s\) would be distinct proper divisors of \(m\). But \(s\) was defined to be the sum of all proper divisors of \(m\), so it would have to satisfy
\[
s\ge 1+s,
\]
an impossibility. Hence \(s=1\). Equation (1) now gives \(m=q\).

Moreover, an integer greater than \(1\) whose proper divisors sum to \(1\) must be prime: if it were composite, it would have a proper divisor strictly greater than \(1\), and the sum of its proper divisors would then exceed \(1\). Therefore \(q\) is prime. We have proved the required form
\[
n=2^kq,\qquad q=2^{k+1}-1\text{ prime},\qquad k\ge1. \tag{2}
\]

We now study subset sums of the proper divisors of this \(n\). Consider the following two sets:
\[
A=\{2^i:0\le i\le k\}

a\text{nd}

C=\{q2^j:0\le j<k\}.
\]
Every member of both sets is a proper divisor of \(n=2^kq\). For \(0\le i\le k\),
\[
2^i\mid 2^kq
\]
because the complementary factor is \(2^{k-i}q\), and \(2^i<n\) because \(2^i\le2^k<2^kq\). Similarly, for \(0\le j<k\),
\[
q2^j\mid 2^kq
\]
with complementary factor \(2^{k-j}\), and
\[
q2^j<q2^k=n.
\]
Thus
\[
A\cup C\subseteq D(n). \tag{3}
\]

The two sets \(A\) and \(C\) are disjoint. Indeed, since \(k\ge1\),
\[
q=2^{k+1}-1>2^k.
\]
Every element of \(A\) is at most \(2^k\), whereas every element of \(C\) is at least \(q\). Hence no element can lie in both.

We next show that every integer \(x\) with \(0\le x<n\) is a sum of distinct elements of \(A\cup C\), and therefore, by (3), a sum of distinct proper divisors of \(n\).

Divide \(x\) by \(q\). There are unique integers \(y,r\) such that
\[
x=qy+r,\qquad 0\le r<q. \tag{4}
\]
Since \(x<2^kq\), division by the positive integer \(q\) gives
\[
y<2^k. \tag{5}
\]
Also,
\[
r<q=2^{k+1}-1<2^{k+1}. \tag{6}
\]
By binary expansion, (6) allows us to write
\[
r=\sum_{i\in I}2^i
\]
for some subset \(I\subseteq\{0,1,\ldots,k\}\). Likewise, (5) allows us to write
\[
y=\sum_{j\in J}2^j
\]
for some subset \(J\subseteq\{0,1,\ldots,k-1\}\). Multiplying the latter equality by \(q\) gives
\[
qy=\sum_{j\in J}q2^j.
\]
Therefore (4) becomes
\[
x=\sum_{i\in I}2^i+\sum_{j\in J}q2^j. \tag{7}
\]
The first summation in (7) uses distinct elements of \(A\), and the second uses distinct elements of \(C\). Because \(A\) and \(C\) are disjoint, their union is a set of distinct proper divisors. Thus \(x\in\mathcal S(n)\). This argument also includes \(x=0\), for which both selected subsets are empty.

The only integer in \(\{0,1,\ldots,n\}\) not covered by the strict inequality \(x<n\) is \(x=n\). But perfection gives exactly the required representation in this case: the sum of all the proper divisors of \(n\) is \(n\). Taking the subset \(D(n)\) itself therefore shows that
\[
n\in\mathcal S(n).
\]
We have consequently proved
\[
\{0,1,\ldots,n\}\subseteq\mathcal S(n). \tag{8}
\]

For the reverse inclusion, let \(x\in\mathcal S(n)\). Then \(x\) is the sum of some subset \(E\subseteq D(n)\). All divisors are nonnegative, so the sum over a subset cannot exceed the sum over the entire set:
\[
0\le x=\sum_{d\in E}d\le\sum_{d\in D(n)}d.
\]
Because \(n\) is perfect, the last sum is \(n\). Hence \(0\le x\le n\), proving
\[
\mathcal S(n)\subseteq\{0,1,\ldots,n\}. \tag{9}
\]

Combining (8) and (9),
\[
\mathcal S(n)=\{0,1,\ldots,n\}.
\]
This set has \(n+1\) elements. The sequence definition excludes the empty-subset sum \(0\) by subtracting one from the number of distinct subset sums, so
\[
a(n)=|\mathcal S(n)|-1=(n+1)-1=n.
\]
Thus every even perfect number \(n\) satisfies \(a(n)=n\), as claimed.
